name: Population (survey estimate)
plain: How many people live in the area, as the American Community Survey estimates it from five years of answers. It is a survey estimate, not the census count and not the yearly estimate, and below the municipality it has a margin of error.
definition: The total population of the area in the American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates, for the windows 2017-2021 to 2020-2024. A five-year estimate pools 60 months of answers: it describes the period, not one day. It counts everyone the survey counts where they live, people in group quarters such as nursing homes included.
geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico; also 901 barrios, 981 census tracts and 2,555 block groups

coverage.frequency: Four windows, 2017-2021 to 2020-2024, labelled by their last year (2021 to 2024). They share years, so the change from one window to the next is not a trend. Rebuilt with each snapshot (python small_area.py), which adds a window when the Census Bureau publishes one.

method: The observatory reads table B01003 (Total Population) of the Census Bureau's American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year files, for each of the four five-year windows, and works the value out by using its total (cell 001). The same arithmetic makes the value for a municipality, a barrio, a census tract and a block group. The margin of error follows the Census Bureau's formulas: the margin of a sum is the square root of the sum of the squares of the margins of its cells, and a share uses the Bureau's proportion formula. A total that the Census Bureau controls to its own estimate has no margin; the observatory gives it a margin of zero, as the Bureau says may be done, so a share of it keeps the margin of its numerator. A cell the Census Bureau leaves empty gives no value, never a zero. A share whose margin works out to zero (a share of exactly 100%, for example) is published without a margin: the proportion formula would give zero, which would read as exact. The Puerto Rico value is the Census Bureau's own island row. The code is small_area.py in the project's repository.
source_detail: ACS 5-year table B01003 (Total Population), table-based summary files, https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/{vintage}/table-based-SF/data/5YRData/ (vintages 2021 to 2024). The cells used are checked against the Census Bureau's own labels, https://api.census.gov/data/{vintage}/acs/acs5/groups/B01003.json, in every vintage at every build.
how_to_read: In the 2020-2024 window the survey puts Puerto Rico at 3,234,309 people. The largest municipalities are San Juan (336,160), Bayamón (182,469) and Carolina (152,204); the smallest are Culebra (1,387) and Maricao (4,988). Counts add up: the block groups of a tract, and the block groups, tracts and barrios of a municipality, give the figure above them exactly (checked for the population, the housing units and the households in every window). For a headline count of residents with no survey margin, use the 2020 Census count (3,285,874 in the crosswalk) or the yearly estimate of the Population Estimates Program (3,184,835 for 2025, housing.population). In 2020-2024 the margin of error is above 30% of the estimate (the CSV by area marks such values as less reliable; no map or table draws areas below the municipality yet) for neither of the 2 municipalities that have a margin (the Census Bureau controls the other 76 totals and prints none), 47% of barrios, 8% of census tracts and 73% of block groups that have a value.
caveats: It is not the 2020 Census count and not the Population Estimates Program's yearly estimate: three sources with different dates and methods. In the 2026-10 snapshot Puerto Rico is 3,285,874 in the 2020 Census, 3,234,309 in the 2020-2024 survey and 3,184,835 for 2025 in the yearly estimates. Cite the source and the period with each figure.

The Census Bureau publishes no margin of error for the total population of the island or of 76 of the 78 municipalities (only Culebra and Maricao have one) because it controls those totals to its own population estimates. Such an estimate has no sampling error, so the Analysis tab shows no margin for it; it is still the Census Bureau's estimate, not a count of everyone. 900 of the 901 barrios have a margin (Florida Adentro has none: the Census Bureau controls its total too), and every census tract and block group has one.
Of the 82 census tracts flagged in 2020-2024, 60 have no residents at all: an estimate of zero with any margin counts as less reliable. Among the 921 tracts with residents the share flagged is 2%.
Below the municipality the figure is a rough survey estimate: read it with its margin of error and see methods.small_area_estimates for how large the margins are.
Adjacent five-year windows share four of their five years, so a change from one window to the next is not a trend to read closely.

method: The observatory reads table B15002 (Sex by Educational Attainment for the Population 25 Years and Over) of the Census Bureau's American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year files, for each of the four five-year windows, and works the value out by adding the sixteen cells below a high school diploma (003 to 010 and 020 to 027) and dividing by the total (001). A total that the Census Bureau controls to its own estimate has no margin; the observatory gives it a margin of zero, as the Bureau says may be done, so a share of it keeps the margin of its numerator. A cell the Census Bureau leaves empty gives no value, never a zero. A share whose margin works out to zero (a share of exactly 100%, for example) is published without a margin: the proportion formula would give zero, which would read as exact. plain: Out of every 100 people aged 5 or older, how many say they speak English less than "very well".
definition: People 5 and older who speak a language other than English at home and rate their English as "well", "not well" or "not at all", divided by all people 5 and older (table B16004), in percent. It is 100 minus the share who speak only English at home or rate their English as "very well".

coverage.frequency: Four windows, 2017-2021 to 2020-2024, labelled by their last year (2021 to 2024). They share years, so the change from one window to the next is not a trend. Rebuilt with each snapshot (python small_area.py), which adds a window when the Census Bureau publishes one.

method: The observatory reads table B16004 (Age by Language Spoken at Home by Ability to Speak English for the Population 5 Years and Over) of the Census Bureau's American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year files, for each of the four five-year windows. It adds the 15 cells of people who speak only English at home or speak English "very well" (in each of the three age groups, the cell "Speak only English" and the cell 'Speak English "very well"' of each of the four language groups), divides by the total (001) and takes that share from 100. The complement of a share has the margin of error of the share. The Census Bureau does not publish block-group values here. The same arithmetic makes the value for a municipality, a barrio, a census tract. A total that the Census Bureau controls to its own estimate has no margin; the observatory gives it a margin of zero, as the Bureau says may be done. The margin of error follows the Census Bureau's formulas: the margin of a sum is the square root of the sum of the squares of the margins of its cells, and a share uses the Bureau's proportion formula. A cell the Census Bureau leaves empty gives no value, never a zero. A share whose margin works out to zero (a share of exactly 100%, for example) is published without a margin. The Puerto Rico value is the Census Bureau's own island row. The code is small_area.py in the project's repository.

how_to_read: In 2020-2024, 39.2% of the people 65 and older of Puerto Rico were below the poverty level (margin ±0.38), against 38.5% in 2017-2021. The share is lowest in Culebra (22.6%), Carolina (27.1%) and Guaynabo (27.1%); it is highest in Guánica (60.9%), Orocovis (53.6%) and Vieques (52.7%). The margin of error is above 30% of the estimate for 1 of the 78 municipalities in 2020-2024.
caveats: Published for the 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico only: below the municipality the share is flagged less reliable for 64% of the barrios and 57% of the census tracts (2020-2024) (docs/small-area.md). The poverty rate of all ages (housing.poverty_pct) is published for barrios and census tracts.
Small municipalities have wide margins: read Culebra and Vieques with theirs.
Adjacent five-year windows share four of their five years, so a change from one window to the next is not a trend to read closely.

plain: How many people of each age live in each municipality, in five-year bands and in broader age groups, with each figure's margin of error; barrios and census tracts get the broad groups only.
definition: population_age.json holds, for the 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (geo.ids, the last is 72), the count of people and its share of all people (with 90% margins of error, four windows 2017-2021 to 2020-2024) for the 18 five-year bands (0 to 4, 5 to 9 ... 80 to 84, 85 and over), the groups under 3, 3 and 4, 5 to 17, 18 to 24, 25 to 44, 45 to 64 and 65 and older, and the broad groups under 18 and 18 to 44. levels.barrio (901 barrios) and levels.tract (981 census tracts) hold the counts and shares of the broad groups under 18, 18 to 44, 45 to 64 and 65 and older only, in the crosswalk's order. Keys: acs_age0to4 ... acs_age85plus (bands), acs_age_under3, acs_age3to4, acs_age5to17, acs_age18to24, acs_age25to44, acs_age45to64, acs_age65plus, acs_under18, acs_age18to44 (counts), each with a _pct share.
geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico; the broad groups also for 901 barrios and 981 census tracts

coverage.frequency: Four windows, 2017-2021 to 2020-2024, labelled by their last year (2021 to 2024). They share years, so the change from one window to the next is not a trend. Rebuilt with each snapshot (python small_area.py), which adds a window when the Census Bureau publishes one.

method: small_area.py (age_file) reads tables B01001 (Sex by Age) and B09001 (Population Under 18 Years by Age) for every window and level through acs_small.py. A five-year band adds the B01001 groups inside it (15 to 19 is 15-17 plus 18-19; 20 to 24 is 20, 21 and 22-24; 60 to 64 is 60-61 plus 62-64; 65 to 69 is 65-66 plus 67-69), male and female. Under 3 and 3 and 4 are B09001's children in households. A count's margin is the square root of the sum of the squares of its cells' margins; a cell the Census Bureau controls to its own estimate prints no margin and adds none, and a count made only of such cells has no margin (it is not exact). A share is over all people (B01001_001) by the proportion formula, with a controlled total given a margin of zero. The five-year bands add up to all people in every area, and so do under 5, 5 to 17, 18 to 24, 25 to 44, 45 to 64 and 65 and older, and under 18, 18 to 44, 45 to 64 and 65 and older (tests/test_small_area.py). Reliability decided what is published below the municipality (2020-2024): every five-year band has a margin above 30% of the estimate for 89% or more of the barrios and 95% or more of the census tracts, so the bands are for municipalities only; of the age groups, the shares of 18 to 44 (39% of barrios flagged), 45 to 64 (31%) and 65 and older (36%) are flagged for under half of the barrios and are published there, with under 18 (70%), published since 2026-10-06; 5 to 17 (79%), 18 to 24 (89%), 25 to 44 (53%), under 3 and 3 and 4 (99% or more) are not.

how_to_read: In 2020-2024 Puerto Rico had about 101,519 children under 5 (56,644 under 3) and 758,086 people 65 and older (23.4%); people 85 and older were 3.1%. Read each count with its margin of error: a band of a small municipality can be rough (the share is flagged less reliable for 20 of the 78 municipalities for 85 and older).
caveats: Adjacent five-year windows share four of their five years, so a change from one window to the next is not a trend to read closely.
Survey estimates, not a census count: they differ from the 2020 census and from the yearly Population Estimates Program.
A blank margin is never an exact value: the Census Bureau controls the total and some age cells of most municipalities to its own estimates and prints no margin for them.
No page draws this table; the Analysis tab shows the shares and counts of the age groups (Population · People and age), not the five-year bands.
